extracted.intended_audience: employers, immigration attorneys, H-1B petitioners, and other stakeholders affected by USCIS H-1B registration and selection policy
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory guidance and DHS responses to public comments on implementing a wage-weighted H-1B registration and selection process, including decisions about wage-level definitions, SOC coding, scope of exemptions, enforcement, transparency, and implementation timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of OEWS wage levels (no new minimum salaries)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS declines suggestions to set new minimum salaries for each wage level and will use OEWS wage levels (already used in H-1B program, publicly accessible, updated annually). OEWS prevailing wages and wage levels are set by DOL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS does not have expertise or manpower to create a new prevailing wage system that would need regular updates, so creating new minimum-salary thresholds per wage level is not feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wage-level definitions tied to occupation-and-location percentiles
rubrics_metrics.description: Wage levels are based on the OEWS survey wage distribution for a specific occupation and location: wage level I ≈ 17th percentile, level II ≈ 34th percentile, level III ≈ 50th percentile, level IV ≈ 67th percentile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using these wage levels in the weighted selection process takes into account wage variations due to occupation and geography and avoids favoring particular occupations or locations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow six-digit SOC code selection per DOL guidance (no four-digit family mapping)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS declines a commenter recommendation to select the six-digit occupation with the highest median wage within its four-digit SOC family (rather than the six-digit SOC corresponding to the job offer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mapping to another six-digit SOC deviates from long-standing DOL prevailing wage guidance and could cause stakeholder confusion; DHS believes there are sufficient provisions to detect and deter occupational misclassification during registration and declines the four-digit-family approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not prioritize registrations based on U.S. education or degree
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS declines suggestions to prioritize graduates from U.S. universities (or give extra weight for U.S. master’s/higher degrees, top-tier schools, STEM field degrees, OPT completion, or Ph.D. holders) beyond existing statutory/administrative exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registrations/petitions for beneficiaries with U.S. master’s or higher degrees already have increased selection odds through prior administrative changes; prioritizing by degree field or giving additional weighting would be complicated, subjective, and inconsistent with the rule's goal to favor higher-skilled and higher-paid aliens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not exempt international students/OPT graduates from cap or weighting
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS declines to exempt students who graduated from U.S. institutions from the visa cap or wage-based weighting or to create a carve-out applying only to beneficiaries inside the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some students may qualify for the existing numerically limited master's-or-higher exemption under INA sec. 214(g)(5)(C), but DHS lacks authority to expand that congressionally created exemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: No industry- or sector-specific carve-outs or priority weighting
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS declines requests to provide special carve-outs, extra weighting, or quotas for particular industries, 'critical sectors,' or occupations (e.g., AI, semiconductors, healthcare, teachers, small/medium manufacturers, nonprofits, startups, public sector).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carve-outs or special treatment for some industries would be overly complicated, unpredictable, and subjective, and occupations considered 'critical' could change over time; not feasible for annual selection administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not weight multiple employer-specific merit factors
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS declines to incorporate employer-specific factors in selection weighting (e.g., petitioner industry criticality, company size, employer demand, occupational shortages, layoffs, local hiring percentage, employer compliance/credibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying and weighing multiple employer characteristics would be overly complicated, unpredictable, subjective, and may involve determinations beyond DHS expertise; it would add unnecessary complexity and frustrate efficient administration of the cap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not weight multiple beneficiary-specific merit factors
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS declines to weight or prioritize beneficiaries based on degree field, industry certification, founder status, ownership, U.S. work history, seniority, patents/research, references, OPT status, length of U.S. residence, IQ, English proficiency, or number of prior H-1B registration attempts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS views salary as a reasonable, objective proxy for skill; adding many beneficiary-specific factors would be infeasible, subjective, and inconsistent with the rule’s goal to favor higher-skilled/higher-paid aliens.

rubrics_metrics.name: No purchase/auctioning of additional lottery chances
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS declines proposals to allow companies to purchase additional chances in the lottery or to 'auction' registrations to employers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Auctioning would favor large corporations with more resources and raise equity concerns; DHS believes auctioning would be inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: No limit on number of registrations per company at registration stage
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS declines suggestions to restrict the maximum number of registrations a single company or affiliated entities may submit in a fiscal year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USCIS does not adjudicate registrations and cannot feasibly determine affiliation at the registration stage, so limiting registrations would not achieve the intended goal and is not practicable at registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage reporting of wage reduction or misrepresentation via existing channels
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS is unclear on an undefined 'beneficiary-centric appeal process' but encourages reporting instances of wage reduction or misrepresentation to DOL or USCIS via existing channels (including ICE tip form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USCIS will investigate tips and refer cases to DHS components or DOL as appropriate; existing reporting mechanisms should be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen enforcement and anti-fraud measures (comments listed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters recommended increased targeted audits, post-approval/post-activation audits, running post-selection audits against EO wage/LCA data, annual compliance reporting, mandatory post-selection wage verification, verified reporting of work hours/worksite locations, oversight of remote work, upfront SOC scrutiny, increased penalties, bans/caps on serial registrants, and bans on outsourcing/third-party placements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS agrees stronger enforcement is necessary but finds the weighted selection process remains appropriate; many enforcement suggestions are out of scope for this rulemaking but DHS may consider ways to improve program integrity in future rulemakings or policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-selection petition scrutiny and denial/revocation standards
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS officers will scrutinize petitions during adjudication to ensure eligibility, including examining wage level, SOC code, area of intended employment, and consistency with the LCA; petitions based on inaccurate, fraudulent, or materially misrepresentative registrations will be denied or revoked (citing 8 CFR 214.2(h)(10)(ii) and (11)(iii)(A)(2)/(A)(6)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration is not adjudicated; petition adjudication is the stage for verifying facts and for denying or revoking approvals when misrepresentations are found.

rubrics_metrics.name: No pilot program; finalize rule as proposed
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS declines recommendations to implement a pilot program or to test a multi-factor model on a smaller scale and will finalize the rule as proposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS reiterates that multi-factor approaches are not feasible because they would be overly complicated, unpredictable, and subjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: No staggered filing windows by wage level
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS declines suggestions to use staggered filing deadlines or application windows by wage level (e.g., sequential windows starting with level IV).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS believes such changes are unnecessary because the rule is consistent with DHS statutory authority and the proposed weighted selection process is lawful without staggered filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date and implementation timing
rubrics_metrics.description: This rule will be effective in time for the FY 2027 registration period, which is set to begin in March 2026.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS believes publishing the rule now provides sufficient time for employers to plan; DHS will not delay implementation into FY 2028 absent other action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processing time and technical operability expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS does not anticipate the weighted selection process will cause significant adjudication delays; USCIS does not adjudicate registrations though adjudicators will require training and may need additional time to review newly required petition information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule does not change current H-1B filing or registration fees; USCIS is confident the system will be operable for FY 2027 and would take remedial measures if the system is inoperable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency: codified entry multipliers per wage level
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations codify the exact weighting multipliers: a beneficiary assigned wage level IV will be entered into the selection pool four times; level III three times; level II two times; level I one time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters requested publishing caps and selection outcomes by wage level, degree type, employer size, NAICS code, and geography; DHS believes the finalized regulations sufficiently detail the weighted selection process and addresses the core transparency concern by codifying the multipliers.
